title: A New Material Uses Water to Help Capture Carbon
summary: Factory smokestacks puff out carbon dioxide mixed with water vapor, and that wet mix has long been a problem for carbon capture. Now researchers at Oregon State University have built a material that turns the problem around: it uses water to help keep capturing carbon dioxide. The material is called BVR-X. It belongs to a group of materials called metal-organic frameworks, or MOFs. MOFs are materials made from metal joined by molecules called linkers, forming tiny cages that trap gas in a process called adsorption. Inside BVR-X, water and carbon dioxide stay mostly separated in its tiny pores. That stops water from taking the spaces needed to capture carbon dioxide. Kyriakos Stylianou of Oregon State University said water usually makes this harder, but the new material keeps working even in very humid conditions. That matters because many materials fail in wet, real smokestacks, and drying the gases first costs extra equipment and energy. Carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas that traps heat and adds to global warming. In the United States, industry makes up 30 percent of all greenhouse gas emissions, according to the Environmental Protection Agency.
why_it_matters: Cleaner air from factories means a healthier planet for you to grow up on.

background_read: Factories burn fuel and send carbon dioxide, a gas that traps heat and warms the Earth, out of their smokestacks.
Carbon capture is a way of trapping that gas before it escapes into the air, but water in the smoky mix often gets in the way.
The new material, BVR-X, is built with tiny cages that hold carbon dioxide and water in separate spaces, so it keeps working even when the gases are wet.
